title: Electromagnetic induction and alternating current
summary: Learn about flux, Faraday's and Lenz's laws, the generator, AC, the transformer, and transmission.
cards.0.p: The measure of the field lines passing through a surface is called magnetic flux (Φ). Flux is found with Φ = B·A·cosθ. θ is the angle between B and the normal to the surface. The unit of flux is the weber.
cards.0.key: If the surface is perpendicular to the field (θ = 0°), the flux is greatest. 1 Wb = 1 T·m². The normal is the line perpendicular to the surface.
cards.0.once.soru: You hold a loop parallel to the field lines. What is the flux through the loop?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: The lines do not pass through the loop. They flow past it. In this case θ = 90° and cos90° = 0.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: The flux is greatest when the loop is perpendicular to the field.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: In the parallel position, no line passes through the loop.
cards.1.p: If the flux changes, an emf forms in the coil. According to Faraday's law, ε = −N·ΔΦ/Δt. If the flux is large but constant, the emf is zero.
cards.1.key: Suppose the flux in a 100-turn coil drops from 0.02 Wb to 0 in 0.1 seconds. The emf is ε = 100 · 0.02 / 0.1 = 20 V. The minus sign in the formula stands for Lenz's law.
cards.2.h: Three ways to change the flux
cards.2.p: Since Φ = B·A·cosθ, the flux changes in three ways. You can change B by bringing a magnet closer, A by enlarging the loop, or θ by rotating the loop.
cards.2.key: In a loop sliding entirely inside a uniform field, the flux does not change. So no emf forms.
cards.2.once.soru: Without touching the magnet, you rotate the coil in place. Does an emf form?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: When the loop rotates, θ and the flux change, so an emf forms. A generator works this way too.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: Not only B but also the angle changes the flux.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Rotating the coil also changes the flux.
cards.3.p: The induced current opposes the change in flux that creates it. If you bring an N pole closer, that face of the loop becomes N and repels the magnet. If you pull it away, that face becomes S and attracts the magnet.
cards.3.key: The work you do against the opposing force turns into electrical energy. So Lenz's law expresses conservation of energy.
cards.4.h: Finding the Lenz direction with the right hand
cards.4.p: If the flux is increasing, the induced current produces a field in the opposite direction. If it is decreasing, it produces a field in the same direction. With the right thumb along this field, the curled fingers show the direction of the current.
cards.4.svg#0: B out of the page toward you (⊙), increasing
cards.4.key: Look at the change in the flux, not at the flux itself. If the field coming toward you is increasing, the current flows clockwise.
cards.4.once.soru: The field through a loop is decreasing. In which direction is the field of the induced current?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The current opposes the decrease and supports the weakening field.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: An opposite field forms when the field is increasing.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: Since the flux changes, a current and its field form.
cards.5.p: An emf forms between the ends of a rod of length L moving in a magnetic field: ε = B·L·v. If a rod sliding on rails completes the circuit, a current flows in the circuit.
cards.5.key: B, L, and v must be perpendicular to one another. If B = 0.5 T, L = 0.4 m, and v = 5 m/s, then ε = 1 V.
cards.6.p: When the current in a coil changes, its own flux changes too, and the coil produces an emf against this: ε = −L·ΔI/Δt. L is the self-inductance, and its unit is the henry.
cards.6.key: A coil resists the change in the current, not its value. At constant current only the resistance of the wire remains. The L here is not a length.
cards.6.once.soru: You close the switch in a circuit with a coil. How does the current rise?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The coil produces an emf against the rise of the current. So the current takes some time to rise.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: A coil resists a change in current and does not allow a sudden rise.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: A coil slows the change, but the current eventually reaches its steady value.
cards.7.p: A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. As the coil rotates in the field, the flux increases and decreases. The emf also reverses direction like a sine curve. This is called alternating current (AC).
cards.7.key: The peak emf is εmax = N·B·A·ω (ω = 2πf). Rotating the coil faster or increasing the number of turns makes the peak emf larger.
cards.8.h: AC: frequency, peak, and rms value
cards.8.p: The voltage at an outlet varies as V = Vmax·sin(2πft). The frequency is 50 Hz in Europe and most of the world, and 60 Hz in the Americas. The rms value is Vmax/√2. The 230 V at an outlet is the rms value, and the peak value is about 325 V.
cards.8.key: The rms value is the DC value that heats a resistor to the same extent. The rms value of the current is likewise Imax/√2. The direction of the current changes 100 times a second.
cards.9.h: Inductor, capacitor, and resonance in AC
cards.9.p: The opposition of an inductor, XL = 2πfL, increases with frequency, and that of a capacitor, XC = 1/(2πfC), decreases. When XL = XC there is resonance, and the current is greatest.
cards.9.key: The opposition of a resistor does not depend on frequency. In a series RLC circuit at resonance, Z = R and f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)).
cards.9.once.soru: You turn the dial of a radio and pick a station. What is being adjusted in the circuit?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The circuit comes into resonance at the station's frequency. So the current of that broadcast is the greatest.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Picking a station adjusts the frequency, not the voltage.
cards.10.p: A transformer is two coils on a shared iron core. The AC in the primary produces a changing flux, and an emf forms in the secondary. In the ideal case V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂, and power is conserved.
cards.10.key: V₁·I₁ = V₂·I₂. A transformer that steps the voltage up steps the current down by the same ratio. Since direct current does not change the flux, a transformer does not work with DC.
cards.10.etk.soru: Explore the parts of a transformer.
cards.10.etk.noktalar.0.acik: It is connected to the AC source. Its changing current creates a changing magnetic flux in the core.
cards.10.etk.noktalar.1.acik: It carries the flux between the two coils. To reduce heat loss, it is made of thin, insulated sheets.
cards.10.etk.noktalar.2.acik: The changing flux creates an emf here. Since N₂ > N₁, V₂ > V₁. This is a step-up transformer.
cards.10.etk.noktalar.3.acik: It is connected to the secondary circuit. In an ideal transformer, the power it draws equals the power drawn from the primary.
cards.11.p: In a real transformer the windings heat up, and eddy currents form in the iron core. Thin, insulated sheets reduce this loss. The efficiency = P₂/P₁ is always less than 100%.
cards.11.key: In large transformers the efficiency exceeds 95%. If the efficiency is not 100%, then V₁·I₁ > V₂·I₂.
cards.11.once.soru: Why does a working charger adapter heat up?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The resistance of the windings and the eddy currents in the core turn energy into heat.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: An adapter steps the voltage down. The heating is caused by the losses.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: The reversing of AC does not produce heat by itself. Resistances produce the heat.
cards.12.p: The heat loss in the line, I²·R, grows with the square of the current. That is why it pays to transmit the same power (P = V·I) at high voltage and small current.
cards.12.key: Electricity is transmitted over long distances at hundreds of kilovolts, and the voltage is stepped down near the city. If you calculate the loss with V²/R, V must be the voltage drop along the line.
cards.13.p: In an induction cooktop, high-frequency AC in a coil creates eddy currents in the base of the pan. The pan heats up, but the glass does not. Contactless cards and wireless charging work this way too.
cards.13.key: The reader's changing field produces an emf in the coil in the card, and the battery-free chip runs. A cooktop usually works with pans that a magnet sticks to.
cards.13.once.soru: You put a glass pot on an induction cooktop. Does it heat up?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Glass is not a conductor. So no eddy current forms in glass.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: The cooktop heats the conducting base, not glass.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Without eddy currents there is no heating either.
cards.14.p:
• When the flux (Φ = B·A·cosθ) changes, an emf forms: ε = −N·ΔΦ/Δt.
• The induced current opposes the change.
• For a rod, ε = B·L·v.
• A generator produces AC. The grid is 50 Hz.
• For a transformer, V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂, and it works only with AC.
quiz.0.q: The flux through a 50-turn coil drops steadily from 0.04 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the magnitude of the emf in the coil in volts?
quiz.1.q: Put in order the path electricity takes from the power plant to your home.
quiz.1.ogeler.1: A transformer steps the voltage up (154-380 kV)
quiz.1.ogeler.2: Electricity travels far on a high-voltage line
quiz.1.ogeler.3: Near the city the voltage is stepped down
quiz.1.e: Since the loss in the line is I²·R, the same power is transmitted at high voltage and small current. So the voltage is stepped up at the plant and stepped down by transformers near the city.
quiz.2.q: Match each device with what it does.
quiz.2.ciftler.2.1: Creates eddy currents in the pan
quiz.2.ciftler.3.1: Creates an emf in a battery-free chip
quiz.2.e: In a generator, a rotating coil converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. A transformer changes an AC voltage through its turns ratio. An induction cooktop creates eddy currents in the base of the pan. A card reader likewise creates an emf in the coil in the card.
quiz.3.q: The N pole of a magnet is brought down toward a conducting loop lying on a table. Looking at the loop from where the magnet is, in which direction is the induced current?
quiz.3.o.0: Clockwise. The top face of the loop is S
quiz.3.o.1: Counterclockwise. The top face of the loop is N
quiz.3.o.2: Clockwise. The top face of the loop is N
quiz.3.e: The field leaving the N pole enters the loop downward and increases. To oppose this, the current produces a field upward (toward you). When your right thumb points toward you, the fingers curl counterclockwise. So the top face becomes N and repels the magnet.
quiz.3.y.0: If the top face were S, it would attract the magnet. By Lenz's law, the loop opposes the approach.
quiz.3.y.2: Seen from above, a clockwise current produces a downward field. That makes the top face S, not N.
quiz.3.y.3: The loop does not have to move for a current to form. A change in the flux through it is enough.
A:ozet: Push a magnet into a coil and see Lenz's rule. Slide a rod on rails and spin a generator. Read the grid voltage, adjust a transformer, and cut the transmission loss.
A:adimlar.0.metin: When the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a current forms in the coil. This is called electromagnetic induction. Push the magnet into the coil at different speeds and watch the galvanometer.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What does the galvanometer's deflection depend on?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: When the magnet stops, the flux does not change and the needle returns to zero.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: As the magnet speeds up, the flux through the coil changes in a shorter time. The faster the flux changes, the larger the voltage.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Look at the faded traces of your trials. As the speed increases, the deflection increases too.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The N pole of the magnet is approaching the coil quickly. The current that forms in the coil also turns the coil into a magnet.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: What does the face of the coil toward the magnet become?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: If that were so, the magnet would speed up on its own, and energy would be produced from nothing.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The current through the coil forces the coil to behave like a magnet.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The coil repels the approaching N pole and so opposes its approach. The work you do pushing the magnet against this repulsion turns into electrical energy.
A:adimlar.2.metin: For a sliding rod, ε = B · L · v. B = 0.5 T, and the length of the rod is L = 0.4 m. Adjust the speed so that the voltage is 0.8 V.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: ε = 0.5 · 0.4 · 4 = 0.8 V. When the rod stops, the area (A) of the circuit no longer changes. The flux stays constant and the current stops.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: 0.5 · 0.4 makes 0.2. For 0.8 V you need v = 0.8 / 0.2.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Spin the coil at different speeds and watch the voltage on the graph.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What happens when the coil spins twice as fast?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The peaks on the graph get higher too. Since εmax = N·B·A·ω, the peak value increases with the rotation speed.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The waves on the graph also get closer together. Frequency is the number of turns per second.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Since εmax = N·B·A·ω, when the speed doubles the peak value doubles too. The frequency is the number of turns per second, so it doubles as well.
A:adimlar.4.metin: In Europe the grid frequency is 50 Hz. So one period lasts T = 1/50 s = 20 ms. Slide the time and find the moment the voltage first reaches its peak value.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: At T/4 = 5 ms the voltage reaches its peak value of 325 V. The 230 V at the outlet is the rms value: 325 / √2 ≈ 230 V. The voltage reverses twice every period, that is 100 times a second.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: The voltage reaches its peak value in a quarter period: 20 / 4.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the numbers of turns: V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂. The primary coil has 1000 turns and is connected to 230 V. Make the output 11.5 V for a phone charger. Then try the battery too.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: V₂ = 230 · 50 / 1000 = 11.5 V. When you connect the battery the output is 0, because the flux of a steady current does not change.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The power plant sends 10 MW, and the resistance of the line is 10 Ω. The power lost as heat in the line is I²·R. Raise the voltage and cut the loss to one hundredth.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: When the voltage becomes 10 times larger, the current drops to one tenth, and the loss I²·R falls to one hundredth.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: The loss is proportional to the square of the current. To cut the current to one tenth, make the voltage 10 times larger.
A:kapanis.0: When the flux through a coil changes, an induced voltage forms: ε = −N·ΔΦ/Δt. The faster the change, the larger the voltage.
A:kapanis.1: By Lenz's law, the induced current opposes the change that creates it. This is conservation of energy.
A:kapanis.2: A generator produces alternating current: εmax = N·B·A·ω. The grid is 50 Hz. 230 V is the rms value, and about 325 V is the peak value.
A:kapanis.3: For a transformer, V₁ / V₂ = N₁ / N₂. A transformer does not work with direct current.
A:kapanis.4: When the voltage becomes 10 times larger, the transmission loss drops to one hundredth.
